ety.text: From Middle English meeting, meting, from Old English mēting, ġemēting (“meeting, assembly, association, society”), equivalent to meet + -ing. Cognate with West Frisian moeting (“meeting, encounter”), Dutch ontmoeting (“meeting, encounter”), Middle Low German mö̂tinge (“meeting”). Compare also German Low German Möte (“meeting, encounter”), Danish møde (“meeting, encounter”), Swedish möte (“meeting, encounter”), Icelandic mót (“meeting”). Related to moot.

senses.d: The act of persons or things that meet.
ex: Meeting him will be exciting. I enjoy meeting new people.

senses.d: A gathering of persons for a purpose; an assembly.
ex: We need to have a meeting about that soon.
In a meeting with government officials, Moon noted that China was “much more advanced” than South Korea in rain-making technologies, his spokesman said.

senses.d: The people at such a gathering.
ex: What has the meeting decided.

senses.d: An encounter between people, even accidental.
ex: They came together in a chance meeting on the way home from work.

senses.d: A place or instance of junction or intersection; a confluence.
ex: Earthquakes occur at the meeting of tectonic plates.

senses.d: A religious service held by a charismatic preacher in small towns in the United States.
ex: You use ta give a good meetin'. I recollect one time you give a whole sermon walkin' around on your hands, yellin' your head off.

senses.d: An administrative unit in the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers).
ex: Denver meeting is a part of Intermountain yearly meeting.

From Middle English meten, from Old English mētan (“to meet, find, encounter”), from Proto-West Germanic *mōtijan (“to meet”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną (“to meet”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to come, meet”).

From Middle English mete, imete, from Old English ġemǣte (“suitable, having the same measurements”), from the Proto-Germanic *gamētijaz, *mētiz (“reasonable; estimable”) (cognate with Dutch meten (“measure”), German gemäß (“suitable”) etc.), itself from collective prefix *ga- + Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”).

senses.d: To come face to face with by accident; to encounter.
ex: Fancy meeting you here! Guess who I met at the supermarket today?

Yesterday, upon the stair
I met a man who wasn’t there
He wasn’t there again today
I wish, I wish he’d go away[…]

senses.d: To come face to face with someone by arrangement.
ex: Let's meet at the station at 9 o'clock.

senses.d: To get acquainted with someone.
ex: I'm pleased to meet you! I'd like you to meet a colleague of mine.
I met my husband through a mutual friend at a party. It wasn't love at first sight; in fact, we couldn't stand each other at first!

senses.d: To gather for a formal or social discussion; to hold a meeting.
ex: I met with them several times. The government ministers met today to start the negotiations.

senses.d: To come together in conflict.
ex:
Weapons more violent, when next we meet,
May serve to better us and worse our foes.

senses.d: To play a match.
ex: England and Holland will meet in the final.

senses.d: To converge and finally touch or intersect.
ex: The two streets meet at a crossroad half a mile away.

senses.d: To touch or hit something while moving.
ex: The right wing of the car met the column in the garage, leaving a dent.

senses.d: To adjoin, be physically touching.
ex: The carpet meets the wall at this side of the room. The forest meets the sea along this part of the coast.

senses.d: To respond to (an argument etc.) with something equally convincing; to refute.
ex: He met every objection to the trip with another reason I should go.

senses.d: A sports competition, especially for track and field or swimming.
ex: track meet
swim meet

senses.d: A gathering of riders, horses and hounds for foxhunting; a field meet for hunting.
A meeting of two trains in opposite directions on a single track, when one is put into a siding to let the other cross.
A meeting.
ex: OK, let's arrange a meet with Tyler and ask him.
You feel me? You use these phones to set up a meet, go to that meet… and talk face to face, period.

senses.d: The greatest lower bound, an operation between pairs of elements in a lattice, denoted by the symbol ∧.
Suitable; right; proper.
ex: It ſeemes not meete, nor wholeſome to my place, / To be producted, (as, if I ſtay, I ſhall,) / Againſt the Moore. […]
And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone: I will make him an helpe meet for him.

senses.d: Submissive; passive.
